clinicalPearls: A myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by clonal proliferation with progressive marrow fibrosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis, classically producing marked splenomegaly
Typical features include fatigue and anaemia, constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever), and abdominal discomfort or early satiety from splenic enlargement
The blood film shows a leucoerythroblastic picture with teardrop-shaped red cells (dacrocytes), nucleated red cells, and immature myeloid forms
Attempts to aspirate marrow often yield a dry tap because of fibrosis, so a trephine biopsy demonstrating reticulin or collagen fibrosis is essential
Driver mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL are present in most cases and support the diagnosis; additional high-risk mutations refine prognosis
Prognostic scoring incorporates age, symptoms, cytopenias, blast count, and cytogenetic/molecular features to guide management decisions
JAK inhibitors reduce spleen size and constitutional symptoms and can improve quality of life, though they are not curative
Allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only curative therapy and is considered for suitable higher-risk patients; transformation to acute leukaemia is a feared complication
reference.pathophysiology: Primary myelofibrosis originates from a clonal haematopoietic stem cell with dysregulated JAK-STAT signalling, most often driven by JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations. The abnormal clone, particularly its megakaryocytes, secretes fibrogenic cytokines and growth factors (such as transforming growth factor-beta and platelet-derived growth factor) that stimulate marrow fibroblasts to deposit reticulin and collagen. As the marrow becomes progressively fibrotic, haematopoiesis relocates to the spleen and liver (extramedullary haematopoiesis), causing organomegaly and release of immature cells into the circulation. A chronic inflammatory cytokine state produces constitutional symptoms, and clonal evolution can culminate in acute leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary (reactive) myelofibrosis from metastatic cancer or infection
Post-polycythaemia vera or post-essential thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis
Hairy cell leukaemia and other marrow-infiltrating disorders
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for leucoerythroblastic changes and teardrop cells
Bone marrow trephine biopsy with reticulin/collagen staining to grade fibrosis
Molecular testing for JAK2, CALR, and MPL, plus high-molecular-risk mutation panels
BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia
Abdominal imaging to document splenomegaly and extramedullary disease
redFlags: Rapidly rising blast count or new cytogenetic changes indicating leukaemic transformation
Severe anaemia or thrombocytopenia with bleeding requiring urgent support
Massive symptomatic splenomegaly with risk of splenic infarction or rupture
Portal hypertension or splanchnic vein thrombosis from extramedullary haematopoiesis and hypercoagulability
reference.prognosis: Survival in primary myelofibrosis is highly variable, ranging from many years in low-risk disease to under two years in high-risk categories; adverse cytogenetics, high-risk mutations, transfusion dependence, and excess blasts predict poorer outcomes, and only allogeneic transplant offers cure.
pitfalls: Assuming a leucoerythroblastic film always indicates PMF without excluding marrow infiltration by malignancy or infection
Relying on a marrow aspirate alone when fibrosis produces a dry tap and a biopsy is needed
Failing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia with BCR-ABL1 testing
Overlooking prognostic mutations that would prompt earlier transplant referral
Not recognising that a JAK inhibitor controls symptoms and spleen size but does not prevent progression
management: Risk stratification using prognostic scores such as DIPSS to direct treatment intensity
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative option, offered to eligible higher-risk patients
JAK inhibition with ruxolitinib to reduce symptomatic splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms
Anaemia management with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, an androgen such as danazol, luspatercept or red cell transfusion
Splenic irradiation or splenectomy for massive symptomatic splenomegaly refractory to drug therapy
Supportive care including transfusion, iron chelation for transfusional iron overload, and treatment of symptomatic extramedullary haematopoiesis
Monitoring of blood counts, spleen size and blast proportion for disease progression and leukaemic transformation
Haematology-led multidisciplinary care with early symptom-focused and palliative support
